title: Docker Complete Handbook
summary: A fundamentals-to-production tour of Docker: architecture, images and containers, Dockerfile and build optimization, storage, networking, Compose, registries, security, debugging and orchestration, with interview questions on every page.

chapters.title: Docker Complete Handbook
points: What it covers: architecture, images, Dockerfile, volumes, networking, Compose, registries, security, debugging, production
Who it is for: developers and DevOps engineers preparing for work or interviews
Core idea: package an app with its dependencies once and run it identically anywhere

chapters.title: Docker Architecture
points: Client-server model: the docker CLI sends REST API calls to the dockerd daemon over a unix socket (/var/run/docker.sock)
Runtime stack: dockerd calls containerd, which uses runc (an OCI runtime) to create the container process
Linux building blocks: namespaces (pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user) isolate, cgroups limit CPU and memory, union filesystems layer the files
Containers vs VMs: containers share the host kernel, start in milliseconds and are MBs in size; VMs run a full guest OS and are GBs. Containers give weaker isolation
Interview Point: Is a container a lightweight VM? Which kernel features make containers work? What is the difference between containerd and runc?

chapters.title: Images and Containers
points: An image is a read-only stack of layers plus metadata; a container is an image plus a thin writable layer and a running process
Copy-on-write: a file is copied up to the writable layer only when modified, and the layer is lost when the container is removed
Lifecycle commands: docker create, start, stop, kill, rm, plus docker run -d -p 8080:80 --name web nginx
docker run vs docker exec vs docker attach: run creates a new container, exec starts an extra process in a running one, attach connects to PID 1's streams
Interview Point: What happens on docker run? Why is a stopped container's data lost on rm? Why does a container exit immediately when its main process ends?

chapters.title: Dockerfile Essentials
points: Core instructions: FROM, WORKDIR, COPY, RUN, ENV, EXPOSE, USER, CMD, ENTRYPOINT
COPY vs ADD: COPY only copies local files; ADD also extracts local tar archives and fetches URLs, so prefer COPY
CMD vs ENTRYPOINT: ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable, CMD supplies default arguments that docker run can override
Exec form ["node","app.js"] runs as PID 1 and receives signals; shell form wraps in /bin/sh -c and can swallow SIGTERM
Interview Point: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT? Why does exec form matter? ARG vs ENV, and which survives into the running container?

chapters.title: Build Optimization
points: Layer cache: each instruction is a layer; a changed layer invalidates every layer after it, so put rarely changing steps first
Cache-friendly order: COPY package.json, RUN npm ci, then COPY the source, so dependencies are not reinstalled on every code change
Multi-stage builds: FROM node AS build, then COPY --from=build into a slim or distroless final image, so the toolchain is not shipped
.dockerignore excludes node_modules, .git and .env from the build context, which speeds up builds and avoids leaking secrets
Interview Point: How do you shrink an image? Why combine RUN steps and clean apt caches in the same layer? What does BuildKit add (parallel stages, cache mounts)?

chapters.title: Volumes and Storage
points: Three mount types: named volume (managed by Docker in /var/lib/docker/volumes), bind mount (host path), tmpfs (memory only)
Volumes outlive containers and work with docker volume create, ls, inspect and prune
Bind mount vs volume: bind mounts suit live-reload in development; volumes suit production data, backups and portability
Example: docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres, and -v $(pwd):/app for a dev bind mount
Interview Point: How do you persist database data? What happens to an anonymous volume on rm? How do you back up a volume?

chapters.title: Docker Networking
points: Drivers: bridge (default), host (shares the host network stack), none, overlay (multi-host), macvlan (container gets its own MAC address)
User-defined bridge networks give automatic DNS by container name; the default bridge does not
Port publishing: -p host:container maps through iptables NAT; EXPOSE is documentation only and publishes nothing
Example: docker network create app-net, then run the api and db containers on it so the api connects to db:5432
Interview Point: Bridge vs host networking? Why can't containers reach each other by name on the default bridge? What does localhost mean inside a container?

chapters.title: Docker Compose
points: compose.yml declares services, networks and volumes for a multi-container app, started with docker compose up -d
Compose creates a default network where each service name resolves as a hostname
depends_on only orders startup; use healthcheck with condition: service_healthy to wait for readiness
Config tools: env_file and environment, profiles for optional services, override files (compose.override.yml) for dev vs prod
Interview Point: Why can an app fail even with depends_on? docker compose down vs down -v? When is Compose not enough?

chapters.title: Registries and Tagging
points: A registry stores images: Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR, GCR, or a self-hosted registry:2; names look like registry/namespace/repo:tag
Tags are mutable pointers, digests (@sha256:...) are immutable; pin digests or exact versions in production
Workflow: docker login, docker tag app:1.0 myrepo/app:1.0, docker push, docker pull
Tagging strategy: semantic versions plus the git SHA; avoid relying on :latest, which is just a default tag with no special meaning
Interview Point: Why is :latest dangerous? Tag vs digest? How do you reduce Docker Hub rate-limit problems (mirror, authenticated pulls)?

chapters.title: Container Security
points: Run as a non-root user (USER in the Dockerfile); root in a container is risky because a breakout lands as host root
Reduce attack surface: minimal base images (alpine, distroless), drop capabilities (--cap-drop ALL), --read-only filesystem, no-new-privileges
Never bake secrets into ENV or layers, because they stay in image history; use BuildKit --mount=type=secret, or runtime secrets
Scan and sign images: Trivy, Docker Scout, Grype for CVEs; Docker Content Trust or cosign for signatures
Interview Point: Why avoid --privileged and mounting docker.sock? How do secrets leak through layers? What do seccomp and AppArmor do?

chapters.title: Debugging and Troubleshooting
points: First-line tools: docker logs -f, docker ps -a, docker inspect (state, mounts, IP), docker events, docker stats
Get inside: docker exec -it app sh; for a crashing container, override the entrypoint with docker run --entrypoint sh
Exit codes: 0 clean, 1 app error, 137 SIGKILL (often OOM kill, check State.OOMKilled), 139 segfault, 143 SIGTERM
Common failures: port already in use, permission denied on bind mounts, DNS or network unreachable, disk full (docker system df, docker system prune)
Interview Point: A container keeps restarting, how do you debug it? What does exit code 137 mean? How do you find what is eating disk?

chapters.title: Production and Orchestration
points: Production hygiene: HEALTHCHECK, restart policies (unless-stopped), resource limits (--memory, --cpus), logging driver with rotation, one process per container
Why orchestrate: scheduling, self-healing, rolling updates, scaling, service discovery and secrets across many hosts
Docker Swarm vs Kubernetes: Swarm is built in and simple (docker stack deploy); Kubernetes is the industry standard with a larger ecosystem and more complexity
Rolling update flow: build and push a versioned image, update the service, health checks gate traffic, roll back on failure
Interview Point: Compose vs Swarm vs Kubernetes? How do you do zero-downtime deploys? Why must containers be stateless and log to stdout?

chapters.title: Docker Cheat Sheet
points: Run: docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 -v data:/data nginx; docker ps -a; docker stop and rm
Images: docker build -t app:1.0 .; docker images; docker pull, push, tag; docker history app
Inspect: docker logs -f; docker exec -it c sh; docker inspect; docker stats; docker top
Compose: docker compose up -d --build; ps; logs -f; down -v
Cleanup: docker system df; docker system prune -a; docker volume prune; docker network prune
Best practices: pin versions, multi-stage builds, non-root user, .dockerignore, one process per container, health checks, no secrets in layers
